claims.text: At the peak, the radiant in Gemini is seventy-three degrees up in the south.
Under a perfect sky, that is up to a hundred and fifty meteors an hour.
150 meteors an hour in a perfect sky

The Geminids look like they come from a single point in Gemini, the radiant. They do not: the meteors are debris from asteroid 3200 Phaethon, and they all travel on parallel paths. We meet the stream head-on, so those paths seem to fan out from a point ahead of us. At the peak the radiant is 73° up in the south, where the ideal rate is up to 150 meteors an hour.

Image: radar imagery of Phaethon, NASA / JPL / Arecibo Observatory. Positions computed for central Europe (50°N, 15°E) with astronomy-engine. Narration uses a synthetic voice.

review.notes: Re-plan only, no new claims: the meteor overlay was too sparse to show the fan it describes (1.5-2 per second), so it now runs at the schema maximum of 5; the Phaethon radar image is shown whole instead of cropped to 38% of its width, and the NASA credit moved above the caption band. Physics and numbers unchanged: radiant 73 deg at 01:52, 150/h ZHR under a perfect sky, debris from 3200 Phaethon on parallel paths, Earth meeting the stream head-on.
